paras: The lynching of F. W. Adams and "Dutchy" was the hanging of two hunters by masked settlers on the Snake River in Carbon County, Wyoming Territory, in October 1888. Accused of slaughtering elk and deer for their hides and of burning a ranchman's house, the two were taken from a guarded adobe hut and hanged from a tree. Later reports of mutilation, fleeing witnesses and freed suspects led Wyoming papers to call it "one of the most atrocious outrages ever committed in Wyoming territory."

According to a Cheyenne dispatch of October 22, based on a cowboy's report, Adams and his partner were killing game "for hides and horns." On Thursday a ranchman, Tom Johnson, remonstrated with them over the territory's game laws and threatened to have them arrested. That night, the dispatch said, they burned Johnson's house, and Adams threatened to kill him if he interfered again. Robert McIntosh, an old-timer in the region, said instead that they had burned "old Findlay's small haystack."

By daylight Johnson had reached a settlement on the Snake, where about forty men joined him and caught the hunters at a dinner camp. The prisoners were brought back about 7 o'clock Friday night and held in an old adobe hut under armed guard. About 10 o'clock, during a thunderstorm, some hundred men in "crude masks" surrounded the hut, and their tall leader ordered the guards home. The Omaha Bee said the bound men were hoisted by lariats from a "red tree" at the leader's pistol signal.

A further Cheyenne dispatch reported that a settler, Davis Phelps, found the bodies by following the horsemen's trail from the "improvised jail." The victims' horses and hunting dog had been killed, and a coat worn by one of the lynchers lay near the bodies. "Dutchy" was identified as Chas. Lutzier; Adams was described as an Illinois veteran due a $40,000 legacy.

A coroner's jury took up the case, and McIntosh urged the governor to punish what he called "a brutal, cowardly and outrageous murder." He also said they were killed for their cash by fewer than half a dozen men. In Fargo, a brother, J. P. Adams, sent the governor his brother's letters and vowed to pursue the killers "if not with the assistance of the authorities, then without them."

A Rawlins report said that of three witnesses subpoenaed, Joe Miller and Henry Cantlin fled and Harper was found shot dead, and that the coat was Miller's. Three settlers arrested on suspicion were released after their hearing before Hughes, the Snake River justice, dissolved in drinking and fights. A $500 reward was offered, and in December constable J. M. Finley said the lynchers would escape unless one turned state's evidence. Alfred McCarger of Snake River wrote to Governor Moonlight denying any part in the lynching. No report of a coroner's verdict, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The cowboy's account ran from the Washington Evening Star to the Lancaster Intelligencer, often as one sentence. Its headlines cast the hunters as aggressors: "Game-Butchers who Burned a Ranchman's House for Revenge Hanged" in the Star, "Two Incendiaries Lynched" in the Sun, and "Two Brutal Hunters" and "Western Justice" in the Omaha Bee. Digests credited "a vigilance committee" or moved the scene to Colorado.

The October 30 follow-up ran as "Denounced by Some Citizens" in the Star and "Lynched After Falling Heir to $40,000" in the Washington Evening Post. The Platte Valley Lyre first called it "the natural outcome" of lawless border game-killing, then printed a Rawlins letter saying punishment belonged to "officers of the law." The Big Horn Sentinel and Daily Yellowstone Journal reprinted the mutilation report, and the Leader called the lynching "atrocious" but told the hearing as comedy.

The Omaha Bee and Maysville Bulletin put the hanging on Friday night; the Fargo item said "the 21st," a Minnesota digest "the 23d," and the Denver dispatch "Monday night." The Sun had forty men capture and hang them the next day; the Arizona paper had settlers burn their cabin and hang them beside it. Rawlins reports described faces battered and eyes gouged, but Finley, the Snake River constable, said they were "not bruised at all."

reader.title: Lynching of F. W. Adams and Charles Lutzier
bases: Two hunters accused of arson and game slaughter were taken from a guarded hut by masked settlers and hanged (A4, A6, A18).

Adams and Lutzier were hanged by a party of masked men without legal authority (A6, A5) as punishment for alleged arson and game-law violations (A4); even McIntosh's lower estimate implies several men (A32).
The Cheyenne wire (A4, A6), a separate Denver dispatch (A24), Rawlins correspondents (A33, A34) and the Leader (A37, A39) agree that the two were lynched on the Snake River.

accounts.label: Cheyenne wire (cowboy's account)
accounts.gist: Hunters burned Johnson's house after he threatened arrest for game-law violations; forty men captured them; about 100 masked men took them from an adobe hut and hanged them.

accounts.label: Short Cheyenne version (Sun)
accounts.gist: Next day forty of Johnson's friends captured the incendiaries and hanged them; no separate masked party.

accounts.label: Denver dispatch / Western digests
accounts.gist: Hunters warned on pain of death by settlers near 'Snake River, Col.' were lynched; one version has settlers burning their cabin and hanging them beside it.

accounts.label: Robert McIntosh
accounts.gist: A brutal, cowardly murder; the men had only burned a haystack and were killed for their cash by fewer than half a dozen men.

accounts.label: Rawlins correspondents
accounts.gist: Bodies shockingly mutilated, eyes gouged; witnesses fled or died; coat traced to Joe Miller.

accounts.label: Constable J. M. Finley
accounts.gist: Victims were bad men but the murder was unjustified; faces not bruised, simply hanged; lynchers likely to escape.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Game-Butchers who Burned a Ranchman's House for Revenge Hanged' and 'Two Brutal Hunters ... Western Justice' tell the story from the pursuers' side.
'Two Incendiaries Lynched' and one-line digest briefs repeat the arson motive without comment.
Further-particulars wire headed 'Denounced by Some Citizens and the Governor Asked to Punish the Lynchers' and 'Lynched After Falling Heir to $40,000'.
Platte Valley Lyre editorial called the lynching 'the natural outcome' of a lawless border situation.
Rawlins letter wants the lynchers given 'a little of their own medicine'; Rawlins special calls it 'one of the most atrocious outrages'.
The Leader calls the lynching 'atrocious' but tells the collapsed hearing as a 'humorous incident'.

conflicts.note: The Friday date comes from the detailed Cheyenne narrative and fits the Sun's Oct. 21 dateline; the others are digests or secondhand.
Wyoming local papers and officers place it in Carbon County, Wyoming; the Colorado placement appears only in Denver-sourced digests.
